Alveolar‑capillary membrane – thin type I pneumocytes for gas exchange, type II cells produce surfactant: Infection fills alveoli with exudate → loss of surfactant → atelectasis and impaired O₂ diffusion, producing hypoxaemia and dyspnoea.

Alveolar walls (type I & II pneumocytes, interstitium): Necrosis of type I cells produces a cavity; loss of type II cells impairs surfactant, promoting atelectasis and further hypoxia that favours anaerobes.

Pulmonary surfactant system – type II pneumocytes produce phospholipid film: Damage or loss of type II cells reduces surfactant → alveolar collapse (atelectasis) and contributes to stiff lungs; also releases profibrotic cytokines (e.g., TGF‑β).

Pulmonary surfactant system – type II pneumocytes produce phospholipid film: Toxic gases (chlorine, ammonia) denature surfactant → alveolar collapse, acute respiratory distress, and later fibrosis if exposure persists.

Toxic gases (chlorine, ammonia) → direct epithelial injury → loss of surfactant → alveolar collapse → acute inflammatory exudate → chemical pneumonitis → possible progression to fibrosis if repeated exposure.

Alveolar type I & II cells – type I for gas exchange, type II produce surfactant and act as progenitors.: Peripheral adenocarcinomas often arise from type II cells or bronchioalveolar stem cells; loss of surfactant regulation contributes to tumour‑induced inflammation.
Children with surfactant protein B deficiency have a very good prognosis

qs.q: Which specific alveolar wall cell type synthesizes surfactant and serves a vital regenerative role following epithelial injury?
o: Capillary endothelium mediating gas exchange
Type II pneumocytes synthesizing surfactant
Alveolar macrophages clearing foreign debris
Type I pneumocytes forming the barrier
qs.e: Type II pneumocytes are rounded cells responsible for surfactant synthesis and alveolar repair after type I cell damage. Type I pneumocytes primarily form the thin plate-like barrier for gas diffusion.

qs.q: How should surfactant therapy be administered to a neonate with respiratory distress syndrome?
o: Instilled directly into the lungs via a tracheal tube or fine catheter
Given orally in divided doses mixed thoroughly with infant formula milk
Administered intravenously as a continuous infusion over several hours
Delivered topically via an inhaled nebulizer mask placed on the face
qs.e: Surfactant therapy is given by instilling surfactant directly into the lungs via a tracheal tube or a fine catheter inserted between the vocal cords. Intravenous or oral routes are ineffective for delivering surfactant to the alveolar surface.

qs.q: What role do surfactants play when located in the lungs?
o: They act as iron-binding transport proteins
They act as opsonins to enhance phagocytosis
They induce a systemic febrile response
They secrete toxic substances to kill flora
qs.e: Surfactants in the lungs act as opsonins, promoting the phagocytosis of pathogens by immune cells. Iron binding is performed by lactoferrin and transferrin.

qs.q: An infant with genetic surfactant metabolism dysfunction undergoes evaluation for lung transplantation options. Which of the following conditions carries the poorest baseline prognosis?
o: Protein surfactant B deficiency
Desquamative interstitial pneumonitis
Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis
Heiner syndrome with milk allergy
qs.e: Protein surfactant B deficiency carries a very poor prognosis in affected infants. In contrast, children with Heiner syndrome secondary to cow's milk allergy generally do very well once cow's milk is withdrawn from their diet.

qs.q: What is the primary mechanism by which meconium causes diffuse atelectasis through surfactant impairment?
o: Mucus and lanugo form a dense waterproof alveolar barrier.
Free fatty acids strip surfactant from the alveolar surface.
Bile salts directly destroy type II pneumocytes within alveoli.
Cellular debris physically blocks natural lamellar body production.
qs.e: Free fatty acids in meconium have a higher minimal surface tension than surfactant and strip it from the alveolar surface. This deactivates and inhibits surfactant, resulting in diffuse atelectasis.

qs.q: What is the functionally principal phospholipid component of pulmonary surfactant?
o: Phosphatidylglycerol functioning primarily as surfactant
Cholesterol functioning primarily as surfactant
Dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine functioning as surfactant
Sphingomyelin functioning primarily as surfactant
qs.e: Dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine (DPPC), also known as lecithin, functions as the principal phospholipid of surfactant. Phosphatidylglycerol serves as a marker for lung maturity but is not strictly necessary for normal lung function.

qs.q: Where are the individual components of pulmonary surfactant primarily synthesized within the cell?
o: Mitochondria of type I alveolar cells
Lysosomes of pulmonary macrophages
Golgi apparatus of type II alveolar cells
Endoplasmic reticulum of club cells
qs.e: The components of pulmonary surfactant are synthesized in the Golgi apparatus of the endoplasmic reticulum of type II alveolar cells. They are subsequently packaged into multilamellar vesicles in the cytoplasm.

qs.q: When should intratracheal surfactant replacement therapy be administered to a neonate with respiratory distress syndrome who requires assisted ventilation?
o: When FIO2 exceeds 0.40, preferably within 2 hours after birth
Only after mechanical ventilation has failed for 24 hours
Prophylactically to all infants born via caesarean delivery
Only after 72 hours if endogenous synthesis fails to begin
qs.e: Neonates with respiratory distress syndrome who require assisted ventilation with an FIO2 of more than 0.40 should receive intratracheal surfactant as soon as possible, preferably within 2 hours after birth. Waiting 24 to 72 hours would delay crucial intervention and worsen lung injury.

es.q: Describe the composition and synthesis of pulmonary surfactant.
es.m:
- **Composition**: Complex lipoprotein composed of 6 phospholipids and 4 apoproteins, containing 70-80% phospholipids, 8-10% protein, and 10% neutral lipids (primarily cholesterol).
- **Primary Phospholipid**: Dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine (DPPC), or lecithin, functions as the principle phospholipid.
- **Marker**: Phosphatidylglycerol makes up 4-15% of phospholipids and acts as a marker for lung maturity, though not necessary for normal lung function.
- **Synthesis Site**: Synthesized in the Golgi apparatus of the endoplasmic reticulum of type II alveolar cells.
- **Packaging**: Packaged into multilamellar vesicles within the cytoplasm of type II alveolar cells.

es.q: Discuss the composition and cellular synthesis of pulmonary surfactant.
es.m:
- **Composition**: Complex lipoprotein composed of 6 phospholipids and 4 apoproteins.
- **Proportions**: Contains 70-80% phospholipids, 8-10% protein, and 10% neutral lipids, primarily cholesterol.
- **Principal Phospholipid**: Dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine (DPPC), or lecithin, is functionally the primary phospholipid.
- **Phosphatidylglycerol**: Makes up 4-15% of phospholipids and acts as a marker for lung maturity, though not necessary for normal lung function.
- **Cellular Synthesis**: Synthesized in the Golgi apparatus of the endoplasmic reticulum within type II alveolar cells.
- **Packaging**: Packaged into multilamellar vesicles located in the cytoplasm of type II alveolar cells.

es.q: Identify factors that decrease the incidence of respiratory distress syndrome as well as conditions causing secondary surfactant deficiency.
es.m:
- **Decreased Incidence Factors**: Use of antenatal steroids, pregnancy-induced or chronic maternal hypertension, and prolonged rupture of membranes.
- **Intrapartum Asphyxia**: Can cause secondary surfactant deficiency.
- **Pulmonary Infections**: Examples include group B beta-hemolytic streptococcal pneumonia.
- **Other Secondary Causes**: Pulmonary hemorrhage, meconium aspiration pneumonia, and oxygen toxicity combined with barotrauma or volutrauma.
- **Structural Causes**: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia and pulmonary hypoplasia.

es.q: → Increased vascular permeability, alveolar flooding, loss of diffusion capacity, surfactant loss (type II pneumocyte damage)
es.m:
**Increased Permeability**
- Damage to epithelium and endothelium increases vascular permeability.
- Protein-rich fluid leaks into the alveolar spaces (alveolar flooding).
- This impairs gas exchange and causes hypoxemia.
- **Surfactant Dysfunction**
- Type II pneumocyte damage leads to decreased surfactant production.
- Surfactant is inactivated by protein-rich edema fluid.
- **Loss of Diffusion Capacity**
- Alveolar flooding and edema thicken the diffusion barrier.
- Leads to reduced oxygen transfer and increased work of breathing.

ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: Surfactant reduces alveolar surface tension, keeping lungs open and preventing collapse. It is produced by type II pneumocytes and is crucial for breathing, especially in preterm infants.

sections.p: Surfactant is a phospholipid-protein complex secreted by type II alveolar cells. It coats the alveolar surface, lowering surface tension and allowing the lungs to expand with minimal effort.
By reducing surface tension, surfactant prevents alveolar collapse (atelectasis) during exhalation and stabilises the lung volume throughout the breathing cycle.
Surfactant synthesis is up‑regulated by glucocorticoids and by the maturation of type II cells. In preterm infants, surfactant production is insufficient until about 34–36 weeks.
Deficiency or dysfunction leads to respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) in preterm infants and can cause acute respiratory failure in adults with ARDS.

t.b: Detects B-lines indicating interstitial fluid; helps differentiate RDS from other causes of respiratory distress
Low compliance suggests surfactant deficiency; guides need for exogenous surfactant

sections.p: Exogenous surfactant therapy is lifesaving for preterm infants with RDS. In adults, surfactant dysfunction contributes to ARDS severity and mortality.
b: Surfactant replacement reduces mortality in preterm RDS

t.b: PaO2/FiO2 ratio <200 indicates ARDS severity; surfactant therapy considered in severe cases
Ground‑glass opacities suggest surfactant dysfunction in ARDS

sections.p: Remember that surfactant is a phospholipid-protein complex secreted by type II cells; its deficiency causes RDS in preterms and contributes to ARDS in adults. Daptomycin is inactivated by surfactant, so it is contraindicated for pneumonia.

whenToSeekHelp: Respiratory distress in a newborn <34 weeks gestation
Severe hypoxaemia (PaO2/FiO2 <200) in adults with ARDS

faq.q: Why is surfactant therapy given to preterm infants?
faq.a: It replaces the insufficient endogenous surfactant, preventing alveolar collapse and improving oxygenation.

faq.q: What causes surfactant deficiency in adults?
faq.a: Severe lung injury, infection, or inflammation (e.g., ARDS) damages type II cells or inactivates surfactant.

faq.q: Can surfactant be used for pneumonia?
faq.a: No; surfactant inactivates daptomycin, and exogenous surfactant has no proven benefit in bacterial pneumonia.

exam: Explain the pathophysiology of respiratory distress syndrome in a 28‑week preterm infant.
Describe how surfactant deficiency contributes to the clinical picture of ARDS.
Outline the indications and contraindications for exogenous surfactant therapy.
